text: You get an m by n board of letters and a list of words. Return every word that can be built on the board. You build a word from letters in cells that touch up, down, left or right. You can't use the same cell twice in one word.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — this is the single-word grid search, but with many words at once. Each word should show up once in the answer, even if the board has it in two places. And the order of the answer doesn't matter. Is that right?
Yes. Any order is fine, and no duplicates.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
The board is at most twelve by twelve. Lowercase letters only. Up to three times ten to the fourth words, each one to ten letters long. All words are unique.

Okay. So the board is small, but the word list is big. That tells me the cost can't be one full board search per word. Let me run through the example. The board is o a a n, e t a e, i h k r, i f l v, and the words are oath, pea, eat, and rain. Oath goes o, a, t, h — right, then down, then down. Eat starts at the e on the right edge and goes left. Pea can't work — there's no p on the board. Rain has no path. So the output is oath and eat. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to run a single-word backtracking search once for each word, starting a DFS from every cell. The problem is that words that share a start, like o a and oath, redo the same walk again and again. With thirty thousand words, that's a lot of repeated work. This problem reminds me of backtracking guided by a prefix tree. If I put all the words in a trie, words with the same start share one path. Then I do one DFS on the board and walk the trie at the same time, so one board walk checks every word that starts with those letters.

Here's the plan. One: put every word in a trie, and let each word's last node store it. Two: for each cell, start only if the root has a child for that letter — mark the cell with a hash sign, search, and restore it. Three: the search carries the trie node for the path so far. If the node stores a word, add it and clear it; then try the four neighbors, skipping cells off the board, already marked, or with no trie child. One thing worth flagging — when I find a word, I don't stop. If the list has o a and oath, returning at o a would miss oath. And clearing the word is how I dedupe, because the same word can be reached from two start cells. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Insert stores the whole word at its last node, instead of an is-word flag. The main loop only starts a search if the root has a child for that letter. Inside search, the check for a missing child is the trie pruning — the same check, one level deeper. One thing worth flagging — the order inside search. I mark the neighbor with a hash sign before I recurse, and I pass node child at cache minus a. I have to use cache there, not the board cell, because that cell is already a hash sign, and hash minus a would be a bad index.

Let's dry-run the code with example one. The trie has fifteen nodes, and the root's children are only o, p, e, and r, so only four cells start a search. Expected: oath and eat. The row that matters is the e on the left edge: the trie says the only letter after e is a, and no neighbor is a, so it stops after one call. That's the pruning doing its job. Nine search calls in total, output oath, eat. That matches. Corner cases: in example two, c isn't next to b, so a b c b is pruned at the third letter — empty output. O a and oath both come out, since a hit doesn't stop me. And on a board a, a, the word a a is added once, because I clear it.

Let me think about complexity here. Building the trie is linear in the total length of all words. The search is m times n times four times three to the L minus one, where L, at most ten, is the longest word. The first step has four ways to go; after that I came from one side, so only three are left. In the worst case the board is all one letter and the words share a long start. On a twelve by twelve board of all a's, with twenty-five words that are nine a's plus one other letter, nothing is found. Per-word search made about forty-seven million calls; the trie made about seven hundred forty thousand, because the words share their first nine letters. Space is linear in the total word length, plus L for the recursion.
Good. Can you make it faster when many words get found?

Follow-up: prune found words out of the trie. After I find a word, I clear it, but its nodes stay, so later searches still walk dead paths. The fix: each node keeps a count of its children. After a node's children are done, if it has no children and no word left, I delete it and lower the parent's count — that's why the DFS takes the parent. When the root's count hits zero, every word is found, so I return early. There's a trade-off here. Pruning only helps when words are actually found. On an all-a board where every word is found, visits drop from about 1.9 million to ten. But when a word is never found, its path stays, the visits are the same, and it's slower. Oh, one more thing — the Big-O stays the same; pruning changes the real work, not the bound.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You moved the DFS from carrying an index into one word to carrying a trie node, so shared starts are walked once and a missing child stops the search. You explained why found doesn't mean stop, and why clearing the word is what removes duplicates. And for the follow-up, you measured both sides: pruning wins big when words get found, but it can't remove anything when they don't. Good work.
